Declined33

Tested and rejected, with the number that killed it. Kept on purpose — a dead idea that stays written down does not get re-proposed every fortnight.

09-02boardIs a BLENDED probability — the card's claim averaged with the hit rates of the slices it belongs to — a better guard than the point score and its five frozen labels? (the bettor's thought: "tip lane hitrates from searches + its original betlane probability / X")
No, and the reason is the most useful thing the test produced. Three blends, each computed strictly as-of like the walker: the plain mean of claim and slice reads (the "/X"), a 50/50 of claim and the slices' mean, and the league base plus the point score re-expressed as a probability. On 62,431 cards, RANKING: the raw claim already separates its top and bottom decile by 12.5 points (12.7 / 11.8 across windows); every blend FLATTENS that to 9.8-11.8, because the slice reads are shrunk toward the league baseline and averaging them in pulls every card toward it. CALIBRATION: the label is the best-calibrated of the five (0.31 points off per decile against 1.08 for the claim) — as it must be, since its rates were measured on this bank; the blends sit between (0.47-0.63). MONEY, which is what a guard is for: the decline rule at 1/p × 1.06 on 8,494 priced cards at best-of-market closing returns +0.93% with the label (+0.87 / +1.03 across seasons, 13 plays a week), and is NEGATIVE for every probability that tracks the card — claim −2.84%, mean −1.76%, half −2.25%, base+ −0.25% — with the raw claim, the steepest ranker, the worst bar. That ordering is the anti-predictive property again: a bar built from a card-specific number finds exactly the cards where the market disagrees with that number most, and those are the cards it is most wrong about. The label works as a bar BECAUSE it is coarse — five category rates the market cannot see through card by card — so the comparison is market-versus-category, not market-versus-Athena. A better probability makes a worse bar here. The point score stays; the blends are declined with their numbers. Instrument: scratchpad blend_test.py
09-02engineShould the cross-division fallback fire on the window's AGE rather than its SIZE? (the patch proposed after the data-hole pass: 17 pending clubs read a window half older than a year while fresher rows sat in the adjacent division, and stale windows graded −2.25 against fresh ones league-controlled)
No — and the −2.25 turns out not to be a data defect the fallback can fix. Three arms, one switch (features.FALLBACK_MODE), same engine: "count" as shipped; "age", which also fires when the own window is half older than a year and next door is fresher, replacing the window; "union", the club's last ten wherever it played them with adjacent rows rescaled. Replayed only where the arms CAN differ — 2,683 fixtures since 2023-07 across the 22 ladder leagues whose own window was stale, unfilled, or older at its tail than the club's newest adjacent row — with abstentions identical (108) in all three. On the 2,575 cards that print in every arm: count 82.10%, age 82.06%, union 81.71%. Age changed the rung on 360 cards and graded 79.72% on them against count's 80.00%; flat (+0.00) in the older window, −0.11 in the newer. Union changed 510 and graded 79.61% against 81.57%; −0.84 older, +0.44 newer — the sign flips, which is the project's definition of nothing. Per league the spread is ±3 points on cells of 60-200 cards, both signs, NED-ED +3.3 next to NED-D2 −3.4. Reading: a club whose own-division window is stale is a club that changed level, and its fresher rows next door carry the exchange-rate error instead of the age error — the two are about the same size, so the −2.25 is the cost of the club, not of the rows. The count gate stays; the switch stays in the code with count as default so the next idea can be replayed against it in an afternoon. Harness: scratchpad age_ab.py, three arms, two windows. Found on the way and shipped separately: the fuzzy matcher joined reserve sides to their parent club across divisions (Jong Ajax read AFC Ajax; Celta Fortuna on the board was priced off Celta Vigo's La Liga form), which would have contaminated the union arm — closed at the matcher before the replay ran
09-01boardShould the guard's price bar be per-league rather than pooled? (the engine is per-league almost everywhere — own goal mean, tempo, floor, shrink, and a consensus cap for seven leagues — while the decision layer judges all 56 competitions against one label rate and one 6% margin, and Serie A's final pick grades a point above pooled)
No evidence it helps, and the reason is more useful than the result. Two variants, both shrinking the league's own record toward the pooled rate rather than replacing it — CELL (league x label) and OFFSET (league deviation applied to every label) — every rate learned on the train half and applied to the test half. MATCHED to the same 1,008 bets so it is not the volume effect: pooled +1.71%, cell prior 100 +0.64%, cell 400 +0.65%, offset 200 +0.07%. At prior 400 the two rules share 88% of their bets and of the 119 they disagree on, the ones per-league ADDS return -1.78% while the ones it DROPS return +7.17%. The mechanism: a per-league bar lowers the requirement where a league historically hits well (Serie A 1.273 -> 1.225), but a league that hits well is one the MARKET also knows hits well and whose prices are already short — so the adjustment admits short-priced bets in efficient markets and excludes the long-priced ones carrying the value. The bar works BECAUSE it is uniform and the market is not: it judges the price against a fixed reference, and market disagreement is the whole signal, so moving the reference toward the league's own record cancels what is being measured. CAVEAT that stops this being a clean rejection: pooled's advantage is one window — older +0.62 against cell-400's +0.79, where per-league is BETTER, and newer +2.80 against +0.52 — which is the single-window pattern that has killed six hypotheses here and gets no exemption. Pooled stays because it is simpler and already shipped, not because it won. Separately worth recording: per-league fairness already lives in the ENGINE, where it belongs — Serie A carries its own goal mean, tempo_factor 0.40 against the 0.50 default, a floor raised to 0.78, a relative-overreach debit against its own base rate, and the consensus cap, and the confluence score reads its own baseline and its own side split (1,295 of 1,483 cards are unders at 87.6% against overs at 76.7%)
09-01boardWhen the starred lane is struck on PRICE, should the card fall back to the other main lane if that one clears its own bar? (the bettor's rule from the Swansea card — tip 1 declined at 1.12 against a needed 1.27, so the DNB at 1.49 is next in line. NOT the score-conditional pivot already rejected: this one fires only on price, and price-conditional selection is the only thing here that has ever paid)
No, and it fails in the most informative way available. On 8,121 priced cards with 2,476 carrying a priced fallback, the star bar at +6% alone returns +1.71% on 1,008 bets; adding the fallback at any margin drags the book to -0.49% or worse, and the fallback bets ALONE return -3.53% on 733 at a 41.5% hit rate against an average CLAIM of 72.2% — a thirty-point overclaim. Loosening the fallback bar HELPS (-3.53% at +0% against -6.35% at +12%), which is the tell. Sliced by how far the price sits above what the claim demands, the claim stays flat near 72% while reality collapses monotonically: +0-5% over break-even hits 52.7% (+1.03%), +5-15% hits 44.1% (+0.09%), +15-35% hits 37.2% (-5.01%), +35%+ hits 25.7% (-16.60%). Both windows agree (-3.82% older, -3.24% newer). THE LESSON, which is worth more than the rejection: a bar of the form 'price >= 1/rate x margin' selects cards where the market disagrees with `rate` most. If rate is a VALIDATED hit rate that finds market error (+1.71%); if rate is the engine's own printed claim it finds ENGINE error (-3.53%), and the harder the bar the more of it you buy. Same arithmetic, opposite sign, and the only difference is whether the denominator was ever measured. This is the sixth confirmation of the anti-predictive property and the purest one. It is why the card marks non-starred lanes claim-based. Also corrected here: the +0.83% previously quoted for the star bar included red-labelled cards, which the card already refuses — excluding them as it actually does gives +1.71%, so the shipped rule was being understated
09-01boardAre thin markets softer, so the final pick can pay there even though it cannot in Europe? (the framing behind the two best live overlays — Jong PSV at 1.44 against a 1.21 consensus, and America-MG U3.5)
No, and the premise is wrong on the market we actually bet. Backfilled the-odds-api across BRA-SB, CHI-PD and SAU-PL — three leagues with no football-data feed at all — for ~3,200 credits and 239 snapshots, deliberately excluding the UEFA cups as the most liquid markets on the board. On 854 graded picks: thin-league TOTALS carry 5.09% overround at the best price across real books (n=1,763) against Europe's 5.60% — slightly TIGHTER, not wider. The fat margin is on 1X2 at 8.53% (n=8,390), which is a genuinely soft market, but the ladder is where the picker spends most of its plays. A small book copies a good totals line, because totals are trivial to arbitrage, and works its margin into the result market instead. Returns follow: -2.90% +/-1.36 there against Europe's -1.70%, on a HIGHER hitrate (85.9% vs 82.1%) at a SHORTER average price (1.12 vs 1.15) — these books know which matches are safe. BRA-SB -3.38%, CHI-PD -1.41%. Dropping red makes it worse (-3.13%) because red is 18 of 854 cards. What this does NOT close: NED-D2, the reserve league that produced the 1.44-vs-1.21 gap, is carried by neither feed and stays unmeasured. Two anecdotes were framed as a strategy ahead of their evidence; what survives is only that the edge, if any, sits in markets too thin for anyone to sell data on
09-01boardDoes the shot-blended forecast turn its better Brier into ROI? (at short prices its edge gradient ran the RIGHT way for the first time — -1.29% at 2 points of claimed edge rising to +3.35% at ten)
No. The gradient was one hot window. Split by date over 1,936 fixtures carrying both a blended forecast and a market line, the entire positive result sits in the older half and the newer half is negative at EVERY threshold: at 5 points of edge +5.51% older against -7.41% newer, at 8 +12.16% against -5.49%, at 10 +18.30% against -8.51%, at 12 +22.15% against -11.11%. The newer half also gets WORSE as the edge bar rises, which is the same anti-predictive shape every other lane family showed, and the hitrate on one identical rule runs 83.7% older against 65.5% newer. What survives is only the accuracy claim, which was validated separately: the blend closes 33% of the Brier gap to the market on this same joined sample. Better forecasting and better betting remain measurably different things
09-01boardShould the chooser look the card's PROFILE up in the bank and take whichever lane has graded best on similar cards? (the bettor's proposal: filter by league plus each lane's kind and probability, then also by home and away side, and let the empirical hitrates pick)
Built and replayed walk-forward over 17,995 cards — each card sees only its own league's earlier matches, never itself or anything later. It loses to simply always taking tip 1 in every configuration: 82.45% at a +/-3 claim band against always-tip-1's 83.64%, and 82.2-83.2% across bands of 2 to 8 and sample floors of 15 to 50. Restricting the neighbourhood to the two clubs made it WORSE (82.20%), as the team-persistence measurement predicts. The cause is estimator quality, not the idea: a neighbourhood hitrate re-estimates a lane's probability from 30-100 cards, where the printed claim is built from thousands, so the lookup swaps a good estimate for a noisier one and then acts on the noise. This is also why the manual filter searches feel so informative and do not convert — they re-derive a number the card already prints
08-31engineDoes tip 2's KIND say which other lane to trust? (the bettor read it off the filter: team-over cards showed tip 1 at 91% and tip 3 at 80%, team-under cards the reverse at 72% and 92%)
No. Replayed over 16,583 fixtures with tip 2's market in the dump: tip 1 is essentially INVARIANT to tip 2's kind — 82.7 on team-over cards, 83.1 on team-under, 84.7 ladder-over, 83.3 ladder-under, 84.4 with no tip 2 at all. A two-point range across four thousand-fixture buckets. The session's 91-versus-72 split was a 20-point gap between samples of 89 and 18 in a goal-heavy week. One real thing did fall out: tip 3's reliability DOES move with tip 2's kind (82.1 on team-over cards against 73.9 on ladder-over), but it never overtakes tip 1, so it changes nothing about the chooser. The proposed mechanism — a team under implying a decisive match — was a story fitted to noise
08-31boardShould the chooser prefer a different lane PER LEAGUE? (the bettor read it off the new filter counters: tip 1 strong in England/Italy/MLS, tip 3 in Germany, tip 2 in France, tip 3 in Norway)
Measured two ways and declined. (1) The 300-match replay per league disagrees with most of it: tip 1 leads in 18 of 20 leagues, including Germany (86.0 vs 80.3) and France (79.9 vs 66.4) where the session slice said otherwise. Only BRA-SA and NOR-EL show tip 3 ahead — Norway 85.4 vs 83.9, the one country read the replay corroborates. (2) The chooser variant scored out of sample (learn each league's best lane on its older half, score on the newer): 83.61% against always-tip-1's 83.71%. Learning the preference buys nothing even when it is allowed to learn. The cause is sample size: a session slice of 18 lanes at 80% carries a standard error of 9.4 points, so a 15-point country gap is one noisy weekend. The counters are a fine lens for spotting questions and a poor one for answering them — which is why the replay exists
08-30boardFinal picking: is the card's starred lane better than always taking tip 1?
No — measured before trusting it. The star's chooser replayed per league at n=300 (16,554 graded fixtures, bank freshly merged with the board's own results): league-average 79.5% against always-tip-1's 83.5%. Every deviation costs — tip 2 picks grade 72.6 where tip 1 would have graded 85.3 (−12.7), tip 3 picks 77.2 vs 83.1 (−5.9). The finding underneath is the valuable one: a tip 1 that MISSES the playable bar still lands 84.5%, because a thin edge means the league's baseline is already high, not that the tip is weak. The star stays (one preferred lane per card was the ask) but now yields to any playable tip 1, and is labelled read-first rather than best-bet — the buy≥ bracket decides what to buy. The About protocol's step 2 was corrected the same day it was written
08-29engineA min or max stated-probability filter on the tips would lift the hitrate
Banded says-vs-hit on the current dumps, last 300 per league, two half-windows: Tip 1 calibrates at every band (worst −1.4, the 70-75 band OVER-delivers +5.7/+2.5), and the team lanes behind Tip 2's cold tile calibrate too — the O1.5s claiming 55-65 hit 58 on a 59 claim in BOTH halves. Nothing overclaims consistently at either end, so a probability cut would only refuse honest low-claim lanes to flatter the tile — the GRE-SL floor mirage again. Declined; instead the tiles now print the family's average CLAIM beside its hit (tip 2: 63.3 vs claims 69.0), so a low number reads as what it promised, not as failure

About

Mission: give the best possible accuracy on value bets.

ATHENA is the engine — a prediction machine that reads nothing but results: goals scored, goals conceded, when, where, against whom. It never sees a bookmaker's odds when it predicts; prices only enter afterwards, to decide whether a prediction is worth money.

TEMPO GUARD is Athena translated to football: the over/under goals market. It estimates how many goals a match should produce, offers the two best rungs on the totals ladder as Tip 1 and Tip 2, and states — honestly — how confident it is and what price makes each tip worth buying (the buy≥ number). Athena itself is sport-agnostic; later builds could point the same engine at other sports.

How to read the board: a playable lane is a tip whose stated probability beats a typical match by more than 1% — the ones with real edge. Found bets are positions actually taken, settled at real prices. Everything on every page is computed from three small data files; no number is ever typed by hand, so nothing can quietly go stale.

What Athena can read

⚽
Team scoring & concedingevery goal for and against, split by home and away, blended with the opponent's defence
📈
Team form recent matches weigh more than old ones, and a scoring streak that breaks from a team's own record is treated with suspicion
🏟️
League cultureseach league has its own goal rhythm — a 2.1-goal league and a 3.2-goal league are priced as different worlds
🏆
International cup culturecontinental ties run on a Club Elo strength lane with their own goal climate — still probationary
↕️
Over & under predictionsthe whole totals ladder, match and team lanes — Tips 1 and 2 are the two best rungs it finds
🥇
Possible winnersthe result lane — double chance and draw no bet as Tip 3, on probation until live results confirm it
🎯
Team totals one side's goals alone — sometimes the strongest signal is that a single team scores, whatever the other does
🧮
Honest probabilitiesdebits, caps and floors measured on two separate time windows before any of them is allowed to ship
💰
Prices as a decision layer onlyodds never touch a prediction — they only decide, afterwards, whether a tip is worth buying

How the board is played — the rules of PRE-ALFA 2

Written down 2 Sep at the reset, from what two runs and the odds layer measured. Session #6 plays these and changes nothing while it runs. Six rules, in order:

1. The verdict line is the whole decision. Every card marks one lane — tip 1, or a draw-no-bet on tip 3 that out-claims it by two points — and the guard reads that lane into one of five labels from the card's own tier and its confluence score, the card run back through the board's searches as-of. Each label carries one measured hit rate, frozen on two windows over 62,528 replayed picks. The card says PLAY only when the best live quote clears that label's break-even by 6% and the tier is not red. That is a bet. Anything else on the board is graded and banked, not played.

2. Flat 4% of the bankroll as it stands. Measured again this session through two seasons at real closing prices: the whole book at 4% is a coin flip with a near-halving drawdown; the STRONG lane compounds (€50 to €106, every year-long start above €50). So the stake is flat, and the volume is low — the target is a few plays a week, not fifteen.

3. STRONG first. A play whose confluence score sits in the top quarter in a European league landed 81.0% at +8.87% on the 1,008 bets the bar fires on, against 72.8% and −0.67% for the rest. Never skip a strong card for price if any book you hold clears its bar.

4. Decide at first sight, buy later if it drifts out. On the same 8,506 cards the early line is lower than the close 61% of the time — the market drifts away from Athena's side toward kickoff — but cards that clear the bar only because the price drifted out late lost in both seasons at both books. A card that does not clear on Thursday is not a play on Saturday; a card that did may be bought at Saturday's longer price.

5. The bar is a category, not the card. Every attempt to bet on Athena's own number — the claim, a blend of claim and searches, an inverse play, per-league bars — lost at real prices, because the market disagrees with Athena most exactly where Athena is most wrong. The five coarse labels are the only bar that has stayed positive in both seasons, and they stay coarse on purpose.

6. The line that reaches the slip. U3.0 is bought as U3.5 and U4.25 as U4.5 — the engine cannot tell those apart and the safer line pays more on settlement; everything else as printed. A match that has kicked off is not playable. Tip 2 and double chance are never played. Where no feed carries a league (Swiss, Polish, Algerian) the score is typed by hand through the same grader as the sweep.

The result lane's own record, kept because tip 3 does not inherit a league's tip 1 weakness:

league tierleaguesavg tip 1avg tip 3
tip 1 under 80%578.7%80.3%
tip 1 80–85%3282.4%79.6%
tip 1 85%+2086.5%78.4%

What it does not see: Athena prices one match's goal total. It has no concept of a two-legged tie, an aggregate score, or what a side needs on the night — and that matters, because a team chasing a deficit plays differently from one protecting a lead. Rather than pretend otherwise, cup cards print the aggregate picture beside the tip and label it context. It also cannot see team news, red cards before they happen, or the weather.

How it stays honest: every constant in the engine must prove itself on two separate time windows before it ships; every era is archived untouched, including the ones that lost money; new lanes (like the international cups) run probationary until live results confirm the backtests. When the engine doesn't know, it says nothing — an abstained match is an answer, not a failure.

Run sessions — how this project is measured

Athena is not developed against a fixed test set. It is developed against runs: a run opens, the engine publishes tips on real fixtures for as long as the run lasts, and the run closes when the slate does. Whatever it scored is then frozen and archived, untouched, and the next run starts from the engine the last one ended with. A run is therefore both the product and the experiment — the only honest test of a change is the next run's number, because that is the only sample the engine has never seen.

Five runs so far, and the arc between them is the whole story:

Pre-calibration · 20–23 Aug 2026Tip 1 landed 84.2% and the run still LOST money — ROI −10.1%. The engine was pricing about 10.8 points optimistic, so every tip was bought at a price that could not pay for its real strike rate. This is the founding lesson of the project and the reason no number here is ever quoted without the price beside it: a strike rate you overpaid for is a loss. Proof in hindsight (27 Aug): this same weekend, replayed through the finished engine, grades 84.2% taking every tip — the losing record was undisciplined volume on an uncalibrated engine, not the slate itself.
First calibrated slate · 23–24 Aug 2026Tip 1 56/65 (86.2%), Tip 2 37/50 (74.0%), and the bets turned positive at ROI +6.1% on 22/27. Five engine defects were found and fixed while it ran, and Rules 1–4 were measured here — buy≥ discipline, flat 4% stakes, the winner's-curse haircut, in-play rung pricing. Those 65 settled tips became the measuring stick every later change is validated against.
Session #3 · 24–27 Aug 2026 · closedThe cup run. Cups had been taken off the board entirely at −11.4, and this run reopened them on a Club Elo strength lane — still probationary. Rules 5 and 6 became numbers, the board became this app, and four separate ideas were measured and declined for the same reason: real signal, no edge. Building the Retrosim page then forced a calibration day: measuring every league at real sample size exposed the old table as mostly noise, found one true engine-wide bias (fixed with a debit), lifted the fourteen weakest leagues with per-league floors — and rolled two of those floors back when the new buy-from column showed their hitrate was bought with unbuyable odds. A page built to display numbers ended up correcting the engine that produces them. Closed at Tip 1 81.9% on 72 settled, found bets −7.5% ROI — the gap between hitrate and price is the lesson the next run inherits.
Sessions #4–5 · 28 Aug – 1 Sep 2026 · closedThe first full run on the calibrated floors, and then the two build days that changed how the board is read: live prices from 26 books, the guard's five labels, the decline rule — the first rule in this project with a positive return at real prices — and the finding underneath it, that the edge lives in the panel and the STRONG lane rather than in volume. Seven missing seasons filled, 552 club spellings folded, five drifted guards closed. Closed at Tip 1 80.9% on 267 settled, found bets −0.3% ROI on 143 — flat, the best a book has done here, and still not the number.
